Lesson 3 · Understand the problem

Sampling, estimation, and hypothesis testing

The baseline identifies a service problem. Before committing further resources, the director requests an independent audit of current shelf availability.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

Auditing all 150 stores is expensive. The team randomly selects 30 stores and checks the same 140 product-days at each during week 16. The question is whether this sample gives a useful estimate of the chain’s current stockout rate. We will calculate the estimate, build an interval around it, and compare that interval with the 10% service target. The audit is a new measurement in the same business, at a later point in the timeline.

Distinguish the population from its estimate

General theory

A statistic varies across samples while its target parameter stays fixed

  • Parameter: the population quantity of interest
  • Estimator: a rule applied to a sample
  • Estimate: the value obtained from the observed sample
  • Sampling distribution: the estimator across repeated samples

Inference asks how a sample informs a population quantity. The estimate is a realized number; the sampling distribution describes how that number would change if sampling were repeated. Begin by specifying the target population, the sampling unit, and the selection design. Those choices determine what repetition means.

The standard error measures sampling variation in the estimated mean

SE(x̄) = s / √n, for independent observations

The standard deviation s describes variation among observations. The standard error describes variation among sample means. Under independent sampling with finite variance, increasing n reduces the standard error at the square-root rate: roughly four times as many observations are needed to halve it.

The law of large numbers explains convergence of the sample mean. The central limit theorem explains its approximate normal sampling distribution for sufficiently large independent samples. When observations occur in dependent groups, use the independent group as the basis for the uncertainty calculation.

A confidence interval combines an estimate with a margin of error

95% mean interval = x̄ ± t₀.₉₇₅,ₙ₋₁ × SE(x̄)

The critical value sets the confidence level, and the standard error sets the width in outcome units. Under independent normal observations, the t interval has its stated coverage; it also provides an approximation in many larger samples. A 95% procedure covers the fixed target in 95% of repeated samples under its model.

Interpret the resulting range against the decision threshold and the size of change that matters. Precision concerns how much the estimate varies, not whether the underlying outcome is large or small.

A sample proportion has uncertainty determined by successes and sample size

p̂ = successes / n; estimated SE(p̂) = √[p̂(1 − p̂) / n]

For independent binary observations, the sample proportion is their mean. The displayed standard error explains how uncertainty depends on n and the estimated share. Wilson intervals improve coverage relative to the simple symmetric normal interval near zero or one and in smaller samples; the worked exercise reports that interval.

Connect the foundations before calculating

General theory

An outcome distribution differs from a distribution of estimates

Repeat the sampling and measurement process to understand the estimator
ObjectWhat varies?Example
Outcome YProduct-day or store selectedStockout indicator or store rate
Estimate from n storesThe newly drawn sampleMean audit rate
Target parameterFixed for the stated populationExpected week-16 equal-store mean

Lesson 2 averaged outcomes using probability weights. Here each hypothetical repetition draws stores and measures their outcomes again; it produces one estimate. The distribution across those estimates determines the standard error. More independent stores usually reduces that variation. It does not automatically remove a biased frame, inaccurate measurement or selective nonresponse.

Choose the information budget before collecting outcomes

Approximate 95% margin m = 1.96σ/√n; choose n ≥ (1.96σ/m)²

Specify the target, independent unit, plausible standard deviation, desired margin and cost before calculating n. This normal approximation treats σ as a planning assumption and observations as independent. A small sample with an estimated SD needs a t-based refinement. Complex sampling, clustering and missing outcomes require design-specific planning; the formula is a starting calculation, not a universal guarantee.

See what repeated sampling changes

General theory

Averages stabilize even though individual observations remain variable

Each observation in this illustration is an independent zero or one with probability 0.4 of one. The first panel is the observation distribution; the next panels are exact distributions of sample means for n=10 and n=50. The observations retain the same SD, while SE of their mean is √[0.4×0.6/n]. The probability of a large error shrinks as n grows: this is the law-of-large-numbers idea.

The central limit theorem addresses a different feature: after centering at the target and scaling by the standard error, the sampling distribution approaches the standard normal under suitable conditions. Here the larger-sample distribution becomes more bell-shaped. The data need not themselves be normal, and convergence is not a claim that every successive realized estimate moves closer to the target.

A confidence level describes the interval procedure across repeated samples

The vertical line is the fixed population mean. Each horizontal interval uses a different independent sample and therefore has a different centre and width. A 95% procedure covers the target in 95% of repetitions under its model; a finite batch need not have exactly 95% coverage. The confidence interval concerns the mean, not a range containing 95% of individual observations. This general illustration does not reveal the retail audit’s known answer.

Estimating variability introduces the heavier tails of the t distribution

When normal observations have unknown population SD, replacing that SD by the sample SD introduces additional uncertainty. The statistic (sample mean − population mean)/(s/√n) then follows t with n−1 degrees of freedom. The raw sample mean is not t-distributed. Small degrees of freedom put more probability in the tails, so a fixed confidence level needs a larger critical value.

For 29 degrees of freedom the two-sided 95% multiplier is about 2.045; the standard-normal multiplier is 1.960. The difference narrows as information increases. This is why an interval calculation specifies its reference distribution and degrees of freedom instead of treating two standard errors as a universal rule.

Test a claim using a specified sampling model

General theory

State the null, alternative, and error costs before testing

  • Null hypothesis: the benchmark claim
  • Alternative: the direction or departure being tested
  • Type I error: reject a true null
  • Type II error: fail to reject a false null

Choose a one-sided alternative when only one pre-specified direction answers the question; choose a two-sided alternative when either direction matters. The significance level controls the probability of rejecting a true null under the testing model. Power is the chance of detecting a specified alternative and depends on effect size, variability, and sample size.

A test statistic expresses distance from the null in standard-error units

t = (estimate − null value) / estimated standard error

Compare this statistic with its reference distribution under the null. The p-value is the probability, under that null model, of a statistic at least as extreme in the direction or directions specified by the alternative. It measures compatibility with the null rather than the probability that the null itself is true.

The relationship between observations determines the comparison test

  • One sample: compare its mean with a benchmark
  • Paired observations: analyze within-pair differences
  • Independent groups: compare group means with their own uncertainty
  • Keep the sampling unit consistent throughout

Pairing uses the fact that two measurements belong to the same unit. A paired t-test becomes a one-sample test of the differences. Independent-group comparisons use uncertainty from both groups; Welch’s approach allows unequal variances. Select the design from how the data were collected, then choose the corresponding formula.

Connect error probabilities with a decision rule

General theory

A test decision can be correct or mistaken in two different ways

Truth and decision are different dimensions
DecisionNull trueSpecified alternative true
Do not rejectCorrect non-rejectionType II error: probability β
RejectType I error: controlled by αDetection: power = 1−β

The significance level α bounds false rejection under the null model. Power is the rejection probability under a specified alternative. For fixed sample size and variability, demanding stronger evidence usually lowers false positives while raising missed signals. Increasing the number of independent observations can improve detection at the same α. Failing to reject is not proof that the null is true.

One-sided and two-sided tests allocate the same error budget differently

Choose the alternative before inspecting the estimate. With α=0.05, a right-sided t test with 29 degrees of freedom rejects above 1.699. A two-sided test splits the error budget between two tails and rejects outside ±2.045. A p-value is the null tail area at least as extreme as the observed statistic in the specified direction or directions. Comparing that area with α gives the same decision as comparing the statistic with the appropriate critical value.

Power depends on the particular difference the test must detect

This deliberately simple illustration uses a standard-normal statistic under the null and a normal statistic shifted by two standard-error units under the alternative. The cutoff remains fixed at 1.645. The area beyond it is 5% under the null and 63.9% under the alternative; power is the latter area. A larger shift increases power. For a fixed difference in outcome units, reducing SE through a larger sample also increases the standardized shift.

These are illustrative normal curves rather than the audit’s calculated power. In a formal sample-size calculation, specify the smallest important difference, the expected variability, the design, and α. A t-based power calculation uses the corresponding noncentral t distribution.

Use repetition and decision thresholds to interpret evidence

General theory

Bootstrap resampling approximates the estimator’s sampling distribution

  • Resample the independent units with replacement
  • Use the original sample size for each bootstrap draw
  • Recalculate the statistic for every draw
  • Use the simulated spread or quantiles to summarize uncertainty

The bootstrap treats the empirical distribution as an approximation to the population distribution. Resampling entire independent units preserves the design information needed for uncertainty. Subsampling without replacement and with fewer observations answers a different repetition question; its raw spread is not automatically the original estimator’s standard error.

Statistical evidence becomes useful when compared with a meaningful effect

  • Report the estimate, interval, and units together
  • Compare the interval with the decision threshold
  • Pre-specify key tests and distinguish exploratory findings
  • Choose additional measurement for the decision it could change

A small p-value can accompany an effect too small to matter, while an imprecise estimate can leave an important decision unresolved. Read statistical uncertainty together with effect size and the consequences of error. When many comparisons are explored, report that search and seek confirmation for the conclusions that will drive action.

Treat the sampled store as the observation

Worked application

Worked application: Independent shelf audit · week 16 · 30 sampled stores. Apply the general method to the shared retail records below.

Six of the 30 audit stores
StoreStockout product-daysProduct-days checkedAudit rate (%)
S0302114015.00
S1491414010.00
S0792614018.57
S00491406.43
S1221714012.14
S1081714012.14

Calculate one rate for each sampled store. Then average those rates. This gives equal weight to each store, matching the chain-level question. The audit records are separate shelf checks rather than a rereading of the system export.

A store contributes many product-days, but those product-days share its delivery process and operating conditions. The calculation below uses variation across the 30 store rates to measure precision. It does not treat thousands of product-days as thousands of independently selected stores.

The baseline in Lessons 1 and 2 covered weeks 1–8. This audit concerns week 16. Keeping the dates visible avoids interpreting a later estimate as a correction to an earlier period’s arithmetic.

Separate variation in stores from variation in estimates

Worked application

A proportion needs its own uncertainty calculation

  • Above target: 19 of 30 audited stores
  • Estimated share: 63.33%
  • Wilson 95% interval: 45.51%–78.13%

This statistic describes the share of stores missing the target, not their average stockout rate. A store is counted once as above or below the threshold. The elementary proportion standard error is √[p̂(1−p̂)/n]; a Wilson interval behaves better near the ends of the zero-to-one range.

Build the estimate and its interval

Worked application

The sample mean is 11.50%. The standard deviation of the 30 store rates is 3.44 percentage points. The standard error divides this spread by the square root of the number of sampled stores, giving 0.63 points.

The standard deviation describes differences between stores; the standard error describes precision in their average. A larger random sample tends to reduce the second quantity. For this small sample, use a t multiplier with 29 degrees of freedom to form the interval.

Standard error = 3.44 ÷ √30 = 0.63 percentage points

95% interval = 11.50 ± 2.05 × 0.63 = 10.22% to 12.78%

Follow this calculation further →

Use the range to judge the service target

Worked application

The whole displayed interval is above the 10% target. That supports treating the current service problem as substantial enough to investigate, while reporting the estimate as a range rather than an exact chain-wide percentage.

The interval procedure is designed to cover its population mean in about 95% of repeated samples under the sampling model. It does not say that 95% of stores lie inside these endpoints. The store distribution remains much wider than the uncertainty in its mean.

The director’s decision is whether more measurement would change the next action. If the entire range is on the same side of the service target, a larger audit may add precision without changing the decision to investigate replenishment. If a costly decision depended on a narrow threshold inside the range, more sampling could have greater value.

See the draws behind the resampling result

Worked application

A bootstrap draw can repeat an observed store

The diagram uses a five-ID excerpt to make replacement visible. It is not the analysis sample. The full bootstrap selects 30 store records with replacement from all 30 audit records and recalculates the mean. The full subsampling exercise selects 15 distinct records without replacement. Preserve the observation being sampled: drawing product-days separately would implement a different design.

The bootstrap histogram places the interval endpoints in the distribution

The standard deviation of these 2,000 means is 0.616 percentage points. Their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles are 10.357% and 12.738%. The distribution is over estimates of an average, not over the 30 individual store rates. The next table compares these endpoints with the analytical t interval.

The percentile method reads endpoints directly from the bootstrap distribution. It does not require that distribution to be perfectly symmetric, but coverage still depends on how well resampling represents the estimator’s uncertainty. More repetitions reduce simulation noise; they do not increase the original audit sample.

Use the observed stores to rehearse repetition

Worked application

Compare analytical and bootstrap uncertainty

Same audit, two uncertainty calculations
ProcedureStandard error95% interval
Store-level t interval0.6310.22 to 12.78
Bootstrap percentile0.6210.36 to 12.74

The percentile interval uses the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap means. Increasing the number of bootstrap repetitions smooths the simulation; it does not create new stores or remove a collection problem. A precise estimate still applies to its specified population, period, and measurement process.

Subsampling answers a different repetition question

  • Select 15 distinct stores without replacement
  • SD of subsample means: 0.62 points
  • Interpret the spread for this smaller sample size

The subsample is smaller and excludes replacement. Its raw spread is not automatically the standard error of the full 30-store estimator. Specify sample size and replacement when describing a resampling procedure. The lab calculates both so their different purposes are visible.

Turn the service target into a testable claim

Worked application

Write the claim before inspecting the p-value

H₀: mean stockout rate ≤ 10%; H₁: mean stockout rate > 10%

The one-sided alternative matches the director’s concern that service is worse than the target. A two-sided alternative asks whether the mean differs in either direction. Choose the direction and significance level before seeing the result. The operational null includes all means at or below 10%; its boundary value, 10%, supplies the reference calculation. Equality of a mean is a restriction on that parameter, not a complete specification of every feature of the distribution.

Measure distance from the null in standard-error units

t = (11.50 − 10) / 0.63 = 2.39

  • One-sided p-value: 0.0118
  • Two-sided p-value: 0.0237

The p-value is the probability, under the stated null model, of a result at least as extreme in the specified direction. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. At α=0.05 with 29 degrees of freedom, 2.39 exceeds the right-sided cutoff 1.699 and also the two-sided cutoff 2.045. Both p-values are below 0.05, so both rules reject their respective nulls. The reported two-sided 95% interval corresponds to the two-sided test; a right-sided test instead matches a 95% lower confidence bound.

Choose the next investigation

  • Many tests; only the smallest p-value is reported. What next?
Discuss, then reveal

Ask for the planned primary outcome and the complete set of comparisons, distinguish planned from exploratory findings, and confirm important results with new evidence. Multiple testing raises the chance of finding an apparently unusual result by chance.

A team tries many outcomes and thresholds, then reports only the smallest p-value. What should the director ask for?

Preserve each store’s two measurements

Worked application

Matching by store and week defines the paired comparison

First four matched stores; difference = audit − system
StoreAudit (%)System (%)Difference (points)
S03015.0017.14-2.14
S14910.0010.71-0.71
S07918.579.299.29
S0046.439.29-2.86

Both measurements concern the same store, week 16, and monitoring basket. Join on store ID after selecting the week, retain only valid matched observations, and check one row per store. The subtraction removes the need to compare one collection of stores with a different collection. The 30 differences, rather than 60 unrelated readings, are the analysis observations.

The distribution of differences shows disagreement hidden by a small average

The average difference is 0.262 points, while the SD of differences is 3.273 points. Positive values mean the audit reports more stockouts; negative values mean the system reports more. Inspect both tails and the observation keys before testing the mean. An average close to zero can coexist with substantial disagreement for individual stores.

The paired t-test applies the one-sample formula to the differences

SE = 3.273/√30 = 0.598; t = 0.262/0.598 = 0.438

Use all 30 paired differences and 29 degrees of freedom. The two-sided p-value is 0.6644; the 95% interval is -0.960 to 1.484 points. At the 5% level, the test does not detect a nonzero average difference. Calculations use unrounded values.

This conclusion does not establish equivalence or close agreement. To assess equivalence, first define the largest acceptable mean discrepancy and use a procedure designed for that margin. To assess agreement for individual stores, study the dispersion of their differences. Here the practical next step is to inspect the measurement process behind the larger discrepancies.

Compare groups containing different stores

Worked application

Independent groups contribute two separate sources of sampling variation

Same audit; variance contributions use different stores
GroupStoresMean (%)SD (points)s²/n
Urban1512.3813.0260.611
Nonurban1510.6193.7000.913

Urban and nonurban rows belong to different stores. Equal group sizes do not create a pairing. Under the independent-groups approximation, the variance of the difference in means is s₁²/n₁ + s₀²/n₀; its square root is the standard error. Welch’s procedure allows the two population variances to differ. The final column is in squared percentage points.

The urban–nonurban interval includes both small and substantial differences

Difference = 1.762; SE = 1.234; t = 1.427; df ≈ 26.94

The 95% Welch interval is -0.771 to 4.295 percentage points, with two-sided p = 0.1649. The 5% test does not detect a nonzero mean difference. The interval also shows that the sample leaves a fairly wide range of magnitudes unresolved.

This comparison describes the audited groups under the stated sampling approximation. Urban location was not randomly assigned, so the difference does not identify the effect of changing location. Compare the workflow with the paired calculation: the target contrast is similar, but the construction of the standard error follows the relationship between observations.

Connect the evidence to its intended use

Worked application

Precision within an audit and relevance to a new setting are separate questions

  • Name the stores, week, measure, and selection process
  • Check whether the proposed decision concerns the same target
  • Compare conditions when transferring to another period or setting
  • Collect bridging evidence when operating conditions change

The interval describes uncertainty for its specified audit target. Applying the result to a holiday promotion, a new product basket, or stores outside this chain requires evidence that the relevant conditions transfer. The week-16 audit is not a correction to the weeks-1–8 baseline. Make the transfer question explicit once, then gather the information the next decision needs.

Searching many tests increases the chance of at least one false alarm

20 independent true-null tests at 5%: P(any false rejection) = 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64.2%

This illustration assumes 20 independent tests whose nulls are all true and whose rejection probabilities are exactly 5%. It explains why reporting only the smallest p-value changes the evidential meaning. Dependent tests need not have this exact probability. Name the planned family, retain all results, and distinguish exploratory findings from planned tests.

For family-wise control, a simple Bonferroni rule compares each of m p-values with α/m. For 20 tests and family α=0.05, that cutoff is 0.0025. The appendix explains this rule and the less conservative step-down Holm procedure. Both address a defined family rather than compensating for an undisclosed search.

Work through the reasoning gap

Worked application

A one-point audit margin requires sixty-two independent stores

Planning SD=4 percentage points; these are assumed inputs, not new audit findings
Illustrative planStoresApproximate marginCost at 25 CU/store
Precision target62±1 point1550
Budget limit40±1.24 points1000

Round the computed sample size upward. Compare the cost of 62 observations with the attainable precision at 40. Measuring more product-days per store may reduce measurement noise, but does not add independent stores or resolve between-store variation. Decide whether that precision is useful for the action threshold before paying for a larger audit.

Two sources of audit variation need two pieces of reasoning

  • The audit selects 30 of the 150 stores without replacement
  • It then takes a fresh availability measurement within each selected store
  • The target is the expected equal-store rate at week 16
  • The displayed t interval is an introductory approximation

Sampling stores without replacement reduces the between-store component through a finite-population correction. Fresh within-store measurement adds another component. Applying √((150−30)/(150−1)) to the entire observed standard error would shrink both components indiscriminately. The existing s/√30 interval is a working approximation; a refined design-based interval must separate store sampling and measurement variation. This limitation belongs beside the main audit result.

Budget for information that could change the decision

Worked application

Report the sampling unit, the audit period, the estimate, and the interval together. Keep the 30 store IDs so follow-up questions refer to the same observations. A useful memo explains what the range changes in the proposed action rather than ending with a confidence percentage.

The next lessons explore how observed operating conditions relate to the stockout rate. They return to the completed baseline profiles so that the comparison is stable while we learn regression. The audit remains a separate piece of evidence about current service performance.

Explain, reconstruct, diagnose and transfer

Decision and synthesis

Reconstruct the calculation before inspecting the worked answer

  • Plan a 95% audit margin of ±1 point using SD=4 points. Compare with a 40-store budget at 25 CU per store.
  • An analyst treats 140 product-days at each of 30 stores as 4,200 independent stores. Explain what uncertainty this would miss.

Work independently or explain your reasoning to a partner. State the target, units and assumptions before calculating. The student notebook provides runnable setup and separate task cells; the companion solution checks the calculation. The lesson’s completed lab remains available as a reference, with its steps separated into smaller cells.

Transfer the method and defend the decision

  • Plan equal randomized arms for a 2-point improvement with SD=4, 80% power and a two-sided 5% test. What changes if stores share a delivery team?
  • Submit a calculation, an assumption and a justified next action

An acceptable answer can recommend more information, a narrower claim or no action. It must connect the method to the target and explain the consequence of a failed assumption. Use the assessment criteria after attempting the task; matching a supplied recommendation is not the grading objective.

After your attempt: check the reasoning

Open the assessment criteria

Round upward to 62 audited stores and 63 per trial arm. State normal-approximation and independence assumptions; cluster planning needs team counts and within-team dependence.

Update the decision memo

The independent week-16 audit estimates 11.50% stockouts, with a 95% interval of 10.22%–12.78%. The range remains above the 10% service target. Proceed with investigating replenishment while retaining the uncertainty in the report.

Make the call

Would multiplying the number of product-days by 30 give the right sample size for the standard error of the mean store rate?

Compare your reasoning

No. The randomly selected units are stores. The standard error here uses the 30 store rates; product-days within a store share its operating conditions.

The bigger picture

The inference framework transfers to audits, surveys, and experimental measurements. Specify the population quantity, understand how the sample was drawn, and quantify the estimator’s sampling variation. The business interpretation then compares the estimate and interval with a meaningful threshold and the cost of getting the decision wrong.

After your decision: open the known answer

The shared world’s expected week-16 stockout rate across all stores is 11.43%. Compare that with the sample estimate and interval after making the decision.
